citation: The first Chicago Catholic church register — Father John Mary Irenaeus St. Cyr's marriage register and his death and burial page — as printed and annotated in the *Illinois Catholic Historical Review*, vol. 4 (July 1921 - April 1922), and republished in two pages by the Genealogy Trails Transcription Team. 128 dated marriages of 1834-1839, each naming groom, bride, witnesses and officiating priest, and 11 deaths and burials of June 1834 to March 1837.
author: J. M. I. St. Cyr, Bernard Schaeffer and Timothy O'Meara (the register); an unnamed contributor to the Illinois Catholic Historical Review (the article and its footnotes); Genealogy Trails Transcription Team (the republication)
date: 1921-1922 (the Review); the Genealogy Trails pages are undated
repository: The register itself was, when the article was written, in the keeping of the parish; the Review is vol. 4 of the Illinois Catholic Historical Society's quarterly. This project has seen neither — only the two web pages.
locator: chicago/4d/data/research/church/text/st_cyr_marriages_1834_1839.txt and chicago/4d/data/research/church/text/st_cyr_deaths_1834_1837.txt, both cached 2026-09-03 and both byte-identical to the genealogytrails caches they were taken from (text/marriages_catholic.txt and text/church_catholicdeaths.txt). Every record's locator names its line in those files. The death page is at https://genealogytrails.com/ill/cook/church_catholicdeaths.html

transcribes.work: The first Chicago Catholic church record, kept by Father J. M. I. St. Cyr from 1833 and continued by Fathers Bernard Schaeffer and Timothy O'Meara to 1839
transcribes.note: THE ORIGINAL, and nobody in this project has seen it. What is read here is a 1921-22 article that prints the marriage entries and the death entries and comments on them. The article itself says the death record 'is contained on a single page' of the book.

transcribes.work: Illinois Catholic Historical Review, vol. 4 (July 1921 - April 1922)
transcribes.note: The layer actually read, at one further remove: the Genealogy Trails team transcribed these two pages out of the Review and this project read the transcription. Every record citing this source is graded transcription_mediated, twice over.

access_notes: NOT RE-FETCHED FOR T-0573. The two pages were cached in text for T-0556 on 2026-09-03 and the cache is what a later run has to be able to trust; tools/read_genealogytrails.py --fetch is how it is refreshed if it ever must be. The reading is taken from the committed copies under data/research/church/text/, which the gate holds byte-identical to those caches.
what_it_supplies: 128 marriages at Chicago (125 of them) between 1834 and 1839, each dated, and each naming its witnesses BY NAME — 513 named readings of people standing at a named place on a named day
six marriages IN THE SCENE YEAR, which with their witnesses put twenty named people in Chicago on five days of 1835
eleven deaths and burials, four of them in 1835, including the death of Thomas Owen, agent of the Indians, at Chicago on 15 October 1835
the register's own arithmetic — 22 St. Cyr marriages, 18 Schaeffer, 87 O'Meara, 1 Plunkett — which verifies any reading of it without the book
the dates bounding each priest's time at Chicago, which is what makes an unsigned entry attributable
the Irish, French and German Catholic population of the town, which is the part the poll books and letter lists reach least well
what_it_does_not_supply: any address, lot, dwelling or workplace — the register places nobody anywhere in the town
any age, except for three infants and one nine-year-old on the death page
the baptisms. The article tallies 282 of them by these same priests and prints none; that register is T-0503's object and is not in this source
residence. A marriage at Chicago on a day of 1835 is presence on that day, and presence is not residence
reliable spelling. The article says so itself: a French and German priest writing Irish and English names, and an Irish priest writing French and German ones
note: THE PAGE IS TITLED 'First Chicago Marriage Records' AND IT IS NOT ALL CHICAGO. Footnote 5 places three of the first four entries — the three of May 1834 — at Bear Creek, Sangamon County, in the home of Hy Durbin, on St. Cyr's return journey from St. Louis, and the article's closing prose repeats it. A reader who takes the page as a Chicago roll plants three households in the wrong town. Those three entries carry the place and at_chicago: false on the rows themselves.
